courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courses.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courses.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
courses.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
courses.contribution: Scholarly sources, argument and research questions in required first-year development.

courses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courses.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
courses.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
courses.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
courses.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis
courses.contribution: Operationalization, measurement, survey and experimental design for empirical language questions.

courses.name: AI Ethics
courses.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
courses.profile: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
courses.topics: Algorithmic fairness and bias; Privacy and surveillance; Responsibility and accountability; Human-value alignment; Moral status of AI; Existential risk and democratic implications; Trust and agency in human-AI interaction; AI in clinical care; Child development and AI; Social and organizational effects of AI; AI in forensic psychology; Cognitive and socioemotional development; AI consciousness and sentience
courses.methods: Ethical-framework application; Philosophical argument evaluation; Psychological-literature synthesis; Theory-based analysis of AI applications; Research podcast scripting, recording and editing
courses.contribution: Actual fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-AI trust and ethical frameworks support critical evaluation of language/data tools. Its psychological project and research podcast are actual methods, not a dedicated language-technology ethics curriculum.

courses.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics
courses.description2: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.
courses.profile: Introduces formal logic, abstract mathematical reasoning and proof. Students analyze propositions and quantified statements, work with sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, and develop direct and indirect proofs. Induction and recursive definitions extend these tools to mathematical structures. The final component systematically models processes and games without chance and investigates the existence and construction of winning strategies.
courses.topics: Propositional and predicate logic; Truth tables and logical laws; Set theory; Boolean algebra and circuits; Quantifiers; Functions and relations; Proof strategies; Mathematical induction; Recursive definitions; Games without chance and winning strategies; Process modelling
courses.methods: Truth-table analysis; Direct proof and proof by cases; Proof by contrapositive and contradiction; Proof with quantifiers; Mathematical induction; Formal process and game modelling
courses.contribution: Predicate logic, proof and recursive structures as tools for formal modelling.

courses.name: Database Management Systems
courses.description2: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
courses.contribution: The current official description establishes relational database theory, SQL, authorization, normalization and query processing. These are concrete tools for structuring and querying a research corpus, not evidence of a linguistic corpus project by default.

courses.name: Software Development
courses.description2: Covers software design, creation, testing and maintenance. Uses C++ and Haskell and covers planning, requirements gathering, testing, deployment and maintenance through discussions and code reviews.
courses.profile: Develops software-construction skills through C++ and functional programming in Haskell, alongside software design and quality assurance. C++ work addresses classes, inheritance, polymorphism and memory management; Haskell introduces functions, recursion, types and input/output. Laboratories apply version control, code review, debugging, testing, documentation and design patterns. Projects require students to build and explain programs in both languages.
courses.topics: C++ classes and operator overloading; Inheritance and polymorphism; Dynamic memory and smart pointers; Copy construction; Functional programming and immutability; Haskell functions, recursion and types; Higher-order functions; Software development lifecycle; Version control; Debugging and testing; Documentation; Design patterns
courses.methods: C++ programming; Haskell functional programming; Git and GitLab version control; Code review; Systematic debugging; Unit and integration testing; White-box and black-box testing; Static testing; Design-pattern implementation; Software documentation
courses.contribution: Program design in C++ and Haskell as implementation practice.

courses.name: Algorithms & Data Structures
courses.description2: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.
courses.profile: Studies algorithm design and analysis, emphasizing how algorithms and data structures affect execution time. Students examine sorting, searching, random-number generation, string matching and graph algorithms, then study computability, verification, reductions and complexity classes. Programming and mathematical exercises develop algorithmic understanding, while projects require students to design, execute and report experimental investigations of performance.
courses.topics: Abstract data structures; Asymptotic complexity; Random-number generation and sampling; Sorting and stability; String matching and finite automata; Sequential and binary search; Graph traversal; Shortest paths and spanning trees; Topological sorting; Computability and Turing machines; Polynomial-time verification; Reductions and complexity hierarchy
courses.methods: Asymptotic time-complexity analysis; Experimental algorithm benchmarking; Algorithm implementation and tracing; Random-number generator testing; Breadth-first and depth-first search; Graph algorithm analysis; Computational reductions
courses.contribution: Algorithms, string matching and finite automata for processing symbolic data.

courses.name: Advanced Algorithms
courses.description2: Studies modern algebraic algorithms and optimization methods. Emphasises algorithmic thinking and mathematical modelling of computational problems.
courses.profile: Studies algebraic algorithms and advanced optimization methods through mathematical reasoning, implementation and experimental analysis. Fast and exact arithmetic, number-theoretic algorithms, matrix multiplication and Fourier transformation lead into hashing, greedy methods, dynamic programming and network flows. Laboratories develop algorithmic understanding, while projects investigate exact computing and optimization, including hypotheses, measured performance and sensitivity analysis.
courses.topics: Asymptotic time complexity; Fast integer arithmetic; Greatest common divisors and modular arithmetic; Chinese remainder theorem; Arbitrary-precision integers; Primality and factorization; Fast matrix multiplication; Polynomials and Fourier transformation; Hashing and Bloom filters; Greedy algorithms and coding; Dynamic programming; Flow networks; Network science
courses.methods: Asymptotic and empirical complexity analysis; Euclidean algorithm; Primality testing and factorization; Fast arithmetic and matrix algorithms; Fast Fourier transformation; Hashing; Greedy optimization; Dynamic programming; Maximum-flow algorithms; Algorithmic experimental design; Sensitivity analysis
courses.contribution: Hashing, Bloom filters, dynamic programming, greedy coding and algorithm benchmarking support efficient symbolic-data and computational-model work. Number-theoretic arithmetic and matrix algorithms are supporting methods, not direct syntax, grammar induction or language-model content.

courses.name: Introduction to Data Science
courses.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
courses.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
courses.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
courses.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis
courses.contribution: Text and web data wrangling and visualization alongside other data types.

courses.name: Machine Learning
courses.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
courses.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
courses.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
courses.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation
courses.contribution: Feature construction, model selection and classification for predictive tasks.

courses.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
courses.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
courses.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
courses.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance
courses.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design
courses.contribution: Direct text classification and generation, transformers and language models within a wider machine learning course.

courses.name: Introduction to Programming
courses.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
courses.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
courses.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
courses.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling
courses.contribution: Python, strings, control flow and functions as foundations for text analysis.

courses.name: Mathematical Methods
courses.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
courses.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
courses.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
courses.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis
courses.contribution: The selected outline establishes calculus, optimization, differential equations, Mathematica and dynamic-model projects. Do not inherit the official description’s linear-algebra emphasis as a claim about this selected offering; actual Linear Algebra is separately selected later.

courses.name: Linear Algebra
courses.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
courses.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
courses.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
courses.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation
courses.contribution: Vector spaces, matrices and transformations relevant to representation and models.

courses.name: Probability & Statistics
courses.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
courses.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
courses.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
courses.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica
courses.contribution: Probability and statistical inference for assessing model results.

courses.name: Introduction to Sociology
courses.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
courses.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
courses.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
courses.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation
courses.contribution: Identity, social interaction and inequality as context for language use.

courses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courses.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
courses.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
courses.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
courses.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation
courses.contribution: Ethnography, interviews, documents, ethics and interpretation for field inquiry, without linguistic elicitation.

courses.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
courses.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
courses.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
courses.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology
courses.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design
courses.contribution: Public spheres and counterpublics as contexts for social discourse.

courses.name: Neurobiology
courses.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
courses.profile: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
courses.topics: Nervous-system evolution and comparative anatomy; Brain cells and morphology; Cerebral circulation and nerves; Animal behaviour and welfare; Sentience and research ethics; Reduction, refinement and replacement; Enrichment and brain development; Regulatory and sexual behaviour; Lifestyle drugs; Circadian rhythms and sleep; Sleeping and eating disorders; Depression and anxiety; Gut-brain axis; Hypothalamus and pineal gland; Dying brain and consciousness
courses.methods: Comparative brain-anatomy analysis; Introductory microscopy and cell staining; Brain-model comparison; Ethical appraisal of animal research and the 3Rs; Literature-based analysis of neurobiological disorders
courses.contribution: Comparative nervous systems and neural anatomy for biological context.

courses.name: Perception & Action
courses.description2: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
courses.contribution: The current official description supports neural mechanisms of perception and action and cognitive-neuroscience/neuropsychological methods. It gives full but bounded support to sensory/processing inquiry, without inventing language-specific experiments or assessment.

courses.name: Higher Order Functions
courses.description2: Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.
courses.profile: Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.
courses.topics: Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Brain structure and hemispheric specialization; Attention and attentional blink; Memory and long-term potentiation; Emotion; Cognitive control and executive functions; Social cognition; Pain; Consciousness; Brain-behaviour relationships; Neuroscience research ethics
courses.methods: Cognitive-neuroscience experimental design; Attentional-blink experiment; Critical analysis of scientific literature and empirical data; Research-proposal development; Scientific peer review
courses.contribution: Official description names language among higher functions; the selected outline concretely establishes attention, memory, control, neural processes, an attentional-blink experiment and research-proposal methods. Treat these as specific cognitive/experimental complements without inventing a detailed neurolinguistic sequence.

courses.name: Psycholinguistics
courses.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
courses.contribution: The current official description directly covers language acquisition, bilingualism, speech comprehension/production, semantics, reading, impairments and language/thought, with hands-on experiments. It supports substantial psycholinguistic contribution; absence of outline enrichment does not diminish those stated topics, while no unlisted EEG/eye-tracker assignment is inferred.

courses.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
courses.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
courses.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
courses.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
courses.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis
courses.contribution: Neuroanatomy, development and learning foundations for psycholinguistics.

courses.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
courses.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
courses.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
courses.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
courses.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting
courses.contribution: Experimental designs and inference transferable to psycholinguistic investigations.

courses.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
courses.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
courses.profile: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
courses.topics: Systematic-review purpose and limitations; Review protocols and scope; Literature searching and inclusion criteria; Data extraction and study coding; Risk of bias; Effect-size types and transformations; Fixed- and random-effects models; Effect heterogeneity; Moderators and subgroup differences; Meta-regression; Publication bias; Research synthesis and reporting
courses.methods: Systematic literature review; Database searching and study screening; Study-data extraction and coding; Critical risk-of-bias appraisal; R programming and data management; Effect-size calculation and conversion; Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis; Moderator and subgroup analysis; Meta-regression; Publication-bias analysis; Meta-analytic visualization and reporting
courses.contribution: Systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing studies of language and cognition.

courses.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
courses.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
courses.profile: Examines physical, cognitive, emotional, social and personality development from prenatal life through old age and death. Biological and environmental influences are considered alongside attachment, education, relationships, cultural differences and developmental psychopathology. Students connect theoretical perspectives to case studies, assessment and interventions at different life stages. A life-story interview with an adult over fifty applies developmental concepts through interviewing, analysis and a written report.
courses.topics: Developmental theories; Genetics and environment; Prenatal development and birth; Infancy and attachment; Cognitive and psychomotor development; Early and middle childhood; Play and education; Adolescence and psychopathology; Emerging and early adulthood; Middle and late adulthood; Relationships and personality development; Care and developmental interventions; Death, dying, grief and bereavement
courses.methods: Life-story interviewing; Theory-guided lifespan interview analysis; Developmental case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of developmental research and assessment reports
courses.contribution: Actual lifespan cognitive/social development and life-story interview methods provide a specific developmental/contextual contribution to acquisition and identity questions; no dedicated child-language experiment is inferred.

courses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
courses.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
courses.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
courses.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
courses.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design
courses.contribution: Argument, rhetorical forms, speech and persuasion in public communication.

courses.name: Dutch
courses.description2: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.
courses.profile: Develops beginner Dutch for everyday oral and written communication while introducing Dutch culture. Speaking and listening receive particular emphasis, supported by pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar, reading and functional writing. Students practise introductions, family conversations, shopping, travel and leisure through dialogues, role-play and short written tasks. Cultural work includes research and presentations in English, engagement with Dutch film and music, and comparison with students’ own cultural contexts.
courses.topics: Dutch pronunciation and spelling; Everyday vocabulary for introductions, family, shopping, travel and leisure; Verb conjugation and the perfect tense; Pronouns and possession; Negation; Main- and subordinate-clause word order; Adjectives, comparatives and superlatives; Functional reading and writing; Everyday Dutch cultural practices; Cross-cultural comparison
courses.methods: Dutch pronunciation practice; Dialogue construction and conversational role-play; Functional writing in Dutch; Comparative cultural analysis
courses.contribution: Beginner Dutch provides genuine pronunciation, grammar, functional writing, dialogue and cultural comparison. It is language-acquisition practice, not parity with formal typology, historical reconstruction or consultant elicitation.

courses.name: Style & Meaning
courses.description2: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.
courses.profile: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
courses.topics: Foregrounding and deviation; Morphology, syntax and lexical semantics; Register and cohesion; Dialogue and turn-taking; Cooperative principle; Speech and thought presentation; Modality and point of view; Transitivity and ideology; Narrative urgency; Figure and ground; Deixis and deictic shift; Schemas, scripts and prototypes; Cognitive grammar and construal; Text-world theory; Negation and lacuna
courses.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence
courses.contribution: Actual linguistic stylistics uses morphology, syntax, lexical semantics, register, turn-taking, pragmatics, deixis and cognitive grammar to analyse retrievable textual evidence. This is real linguistic subject/method overlap, not merely generic communication, but not a full structural-typology sequence.

courses.name: Rhetoric in Action
courses.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
courses.profile: Applies rhetoric through community-engaged work with local primary-school children. Students develop their own public-speaking, debating and storytelling skills, then design and iteratively refine age-appropriate teaching activities with school partners. On-site coaching and a final public-speaking event connect rhetorical education to civic participation and confidence. Structured reflection examines reciprocity, cultural sensitivity, personal development and the practical challenges of community-engaged teaching.
courses.topics: Public work of rhetoric; Community-engaged learning and reciprocity; Public speaking and debate; Storytelling; Children's rhetorical confidence and civic participation; Rhetorical teaching and coaching; Cultural sensitivity; Collaboration with community partners; Experiential and reflective learning
courses.methods: Public-speaking and debate coaching; Storytelling exercises; Iterative design and revision of teaching materials; Practice-based rhetorical instruction; Gibbs reflective-cycle analysis; Public-speaking event design and evaluation
courses.contribution: Applied public speaking and storytelling with community partners.

courses.name: Persuasive Communication
courses.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
courses.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
courses.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
courses.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle
courses.contribution: Message framing, audience influence and persuasive communication.

courses.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
courses.description2: Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own creative work.
courses.profile: Studies and develops creative communication through poetry, performance and critically articulated artistic practice. Students move from lyric foundations to constrained and experimental forms, attending to sound, rhythm, imagery, voice and embodiment. Close reading and creative workshops lead into an independent traditional or hybrid project grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. Revision and reflection require students to justify formal, conceptual and procedural choices.
courses.topics: Meaning and formal experimentation; Lyric poetry; Poetic sound and rhythm; Imagery and voice; Embodiment and performance; Constraint and formal deviation; Experimental poetry; Hybrid and digitally mediated forms; Creative process and revision; Aesthetic traditions and conceptual coherence
courses.methods: Close poetic reading and listening; Constraint-based composition; Poetic and performative experimentation; Structured drafting and revision; Critical analysis of creative decisions; Independent practice-based creative inquiry
courses.contribution: Sound, rhythm, formal deviation and experimental meaning in creative language.

courses.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
courses.description2: Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.
courses.profile: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.
courses.topics: Definitions and value of literature; Literary genre and originality; Story, plot and narrative structure; Character, setting and point of view; Symbolism and allegory; Style, tone, humour and irony; Graphic fiction and microfiction; Creative nonfiction and memoir; Children's literature; Poetic language, imagery, sound and form; Drama and tragedy; Film adaptation
courses.methods: Close reading; Formalist literary analysis; Narrative analysis; Poetic and dramatic analysis; Critical-source integration; Literary essay and review construction
courses.contribution: Narrative and stylistic close reading for textual interpretation.

courses.name: Film & Text
courses.description2: Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.
courses.profile: Studies the translation of literary narratives into film through formal analysis and adaptation theory. Students compare plot, structure, characterization and setting with cinematic image, acting, editing, music and sound. Medium specificity, fidelity, intertextuality, auteurism, heritage and adaptation markets frame theoretical debates. A substantial research project applies selected concepts to literary and film material, developing an independent interpretation and leading a text- and film-based discussion.
courses.topics: Literature-film relationships; Narrative and medium specificity; Fidelity debates; Cinematography and mise-en-scène; Editing, continuity and montage; Film music and sound; Intertextuality; Auteurism; Adaptation and heritage; Adaptation markets; Spectatorship and immersion
courses.methods: Formalist literary analysis; Close film-sequence analysis; Comparative text-film analysis; Intertextual analysis; Theory-led adaptation research
courses.contribution: Cross-media narrative and interpretation, complementary to discourse analysis.

courses.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
courses.description2: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.
courses.contribution: The current official description supports humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural-minority and psychoanalytic interpretive perspectives and a research project applying selected perspectives to texts. It does not establish formal linguistic field documentation.

courses.name: Media & Race
courses.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
courses.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
courses.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
courses.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection
courses.contribution: Media representation, discourse and power in racialized contexts.

additionalCandidate.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
additionalCandidate.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
additionalCandidate.profile: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.
additionalCandidate.topics: Spatial and spectral image representations; Cameras and calibration; Colour models and quantization; Image histograms; Point operators; Linear and nonlinear filters; Edges and contours; Mathematical morphology; Image segmentation; Curve and corner detection; Feature detection and tracking; Object localization and classification; Recognition performance
additionalCandidate.methods: Python and OpenCV programming; Image filtering; Histogram and point transformations; Morphological image processing; Hough transform; Image segmentation; Feature matching and tracking; Recognition-pipeline design; Benchmark evaluation on unseen images
additionalCandidate.finding: Full available evidence considered. Mathematical morphology is an image-processing operation; OpenCV/image filtering, segmentation and recognition pipelines do not establish linguistic morphology, corpus annotation or linguistic fieldwork. No automatic extra concept from the keyword match.

researchProposals.label: Language, Cognition and Discourse
researchProposals.concept: Investigate how people process, interpret and use language, connecting experimental psycholinguistics, linguistic stylistics and discourse inquiry with cognitive and social methods.

researchProposals.label: Language, Text Data and Computation
researchProposals.concept: Investigate language and text as data and computation, connecting actual psycholinguistics and stylistic analysis with text-data workflows, programming, algorithms and models, while critically interpreting their outputs.
